catalog_quote: The most concise description of the basic stress pattern of Munster Irish is given by Ó Sé (2000). I quote this in the author’s own translation (Ó Sé 2008:p. 96): Word stress falls on the second syllable if it is heavy, on the third syllable if it is heavy and the preceding syllables are light, and on the first syllable in all other cases. Coda consonants in Corca Dhuibhne Irish are nonmoraic, as the example in (1) shows: stress falls on the initial syllable despite the second syllable being closed ... In its simplest form the stress pattern of Corca Dhuibhne Irish can be summarized in three principles of varying generality: • Stress falls no further away from the left edge than the third syllable; • Stress falls on the leftmost stressable syllable; • Stress is attracted to heavy syllables; • A heavy initial is not stressed if immediately followed by another heavy syllable. ... sweep_summary: Irish (iris1253) is in the catalog as fixed-strict initial stress (initial stress, Gordon-sourced, domain quote Ní Chasaide 1999 p. 115 'Primary lexical stress is located on the first syllable of most words'), but the deciding quotation held by the project is Iosad 2013 p. 67 quoting Ó Sé 2008: 96 on Corca Dhuibhne (Munster) Irish, which is a weight-sensitive, left-bounded three-syllable-window system. The quotation is verbatim-correct (Iosad PDF now obtained by the project), but it describes the one dialect group that is NOT fixed: initial syllable, so it does not support the classification; the record should either swap its deciding source to a non-Munster statement or split off Munster (Glottolog dialect muns1250) as a separate weight-sensitive unit. Of the 14 title hits (three are duplicate records of Green's Benjamins clitics chapter): read in full this search of works with stress in the title — Elfner 2012 (open diss via the Internet Archive: initial stress in all dialects except Munster; best new statement), Torres-Tamarit & Hermans 2017 (Glossa, CC BY via UAB repository: restates Iosad's Munster data, confirms), Iosad 2013 (confirms), Bennett/Elfner/McCloskey 2015 and 2019 (author preprints from Bennett's UCSC page: phrasal prosody, silent on word stress); held by the project from the earlier reading and re-read — Green 1996 (Connacht/Ulster initial, Munster heavy-attracted; refines: Gussmann-1995 fourth-syllable stress cases against the three-syllable window), Quiggin 1906 §477 p. 152 (Donegal: 'Word-stress always falls upon the first syllable of a simple word'), Ní Chasaide 1999, Green 1997 diss, Windsor/Coward/Flynn 2018 (Munster: left-edge default, shift to a heavy syllable up to the third). Not obtainable: Ó Sé 2008 Éigse 36 (primary; site PDF is subscriber-encrypted, downloaded and deleted unread; priority high), Rowicka 1996 and Gussmann 1997 (print Festschriften, no open copies; priority medium, both disputed by Ó Sé 2008 per Iosad p. 100), Doherty 1991 (PASC 2, not online; low), Green 2000/2001 clitics chapter (Benjamins, closed; low; his ROA-196 diss held by the project covers the stress content), Mac Eoin 1994 (metrical term laíd, irrelevant). searches ran through Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, DOAJ, HAL API, DuckDuckGo/Bing HTML, the Internet Archive.

This supports the catalog's fixed: initial syllable ('fixed-strict', initial stress) coding for Irish as a language-level unit, with Munster as the explicit exception. sources.note: Confirms the catalog quotation verbatim (p. 67). Scope is explicitly the Corca Dhuibhne (Dingle) dialect of Munster Irish, not Irish as a whole: bounded weight-sensitive stress within a left-edge three-syllable window, default initial. Note: this quotation describes a weight-sensitive system, so it does not by itself support the catalog's 'fixed-strict' initial coding; that coding rests on the non-Munster dialects (Ní Chasaide 1999, Elfner 2012, Green 1996 p. 1, Quiggin 1906).

sources.citation: Torres-Tamarit, Francesc & Ben Hermans (2017). Branchingness constraints on heads and dependents in Munster Irish stress. Glossa 2(1): 99, 1-19. doi:10.5334/gjgl.464
sources.quote: In MI long vowels and diphthongs, but not syllables closed by a consonant, count as heavy (H). Morphological structure does not affect the position of stress. Stress is initial in words that contain no H syllable in the first three syllables of the word (1a-c), and no initial light (L) syllable can be stressed if immediately followed by a H syllable (1e-g), meaning that H syllables attract stress. Sequences of a H and a L syllable attract stress to the H syllable (2). In a sequence of two H syllables word-initially, the second H syllable receives main stress (3). If a H syllable is preceded by a word-initial sequence of two L syllables, primary stress falls on the H syllable (4). [p. 3:] The unmarked stress pattern in MI is word-initial.
sources.note: OT analysis of Dingle-peninsula Munster Irish stress; data taken from Iosad 2013 (p. 2: 'The data we present come from Iosad (2013), unless otherwise specified'), so it is derivative of the catalog's own source. Restates the same generalization: initial default, leftmost heavy syllable within the first three syllables attracts stress, HH-initial gives second-syllable stress, [ax] heavy only as second syllable. Confirms the catalog quotation; adds nothing first-hand.
